title: CICO — Declare, and Choose the Technique
keywords: declare it out loud — the commonest cause of death in CICO is delay, not technique
DAS 2025: 3+1 intubation attempts, up to 3 supraglottic, then two-person mask, then the neck
scalpel-bougie-tube is the default adult technique; cannula failed in roughly 60% of NAP4 cases
under 8 years the anatomy changes the answer — surgical tracheotomy, not cricothyroidotomy
sources: Ahmad I, El-Boghdadly K, Bhagrath R, et al. Difficult Airway Society 2025 guidelines for management of unanticipated difficult tracheal intubation in adults. Br J Anaesth. 2026;136(2):283-307.
Cook TM, Woodall N, Frerk C. Major complications of airway management in the UK: 4th National Audit Project (NAP4). Br J Anaesth. 2011;106(5):617-631.
Chrimes N. The Vortex: a universal 'high-acuity implementation tool' for emergency airway management. Br J Anaesth. 2016;117(Suppl 1):i20-i27.
Haag B, et al. Emergency front-of-neck access in pediatric anesthesia: a narrative review. Paediatr Anaesth. 2024;34(10) (age-stratified technique choice).

Disma N, Asai T, Cools E, et al. Airway management in neonates and infants: European Society of Anaesthesiology and Intensive Care and British Journal of Anaesthesia joint guidelines. Br J Anaesth. 2024;132(1):124-144 (surgical tracheotomy first-line under 1 year).

changelog.change: New — the entry point for the CICO & Front-of-Neck Access category created in this batch. Previously CICO existed only as a node inside airway-management-flow and as the opening step of the cricothyroidotomy card, with no place that answered 'which technique, for this patient'. Built against DAS 2025, NAP4, and the 2024 pediatric/neonatal guidance.

purpose: The entry point to front-of-neck access: recognizing and declaring CICO, the attempt ladder that precedes it, and which of the four techniques fits this patient.
entryPrompt: You do not choose a technique in a CICO. You choose it now, before one happens — this card exists so the decision is already made when the alarm goes off.

nodes.prompt: 1 · Recognize it before you can name it
nodes.body:
CICO is not a moment; it is a trajectory you should see coming. The three failures that define it — intubation, supraglottic airway, face mask — usually declare themselves one after the other over a few minutes, while saturation falls and the room gets quieter.

The practical trigger is simpler than the definition: you cannot get oxygen into the patient by any route above the neck, and the saturation is falling. That is enough. Waiting for a number, or for someone senior to say it first, is how the time gets spent.

items: Rising urgency with falling options is the signal. If each thing you try is buying less time than the last, you are in it.
Do not wait for a specific saturation. By the time the number is unequivocal the desaturation is already steep, and in a child it is vertical.

The Vortex framing is useful here: three lifelines — face mask, supraglottic airway, tracheal tube. Each gets a best-effort attempt. When all three have had their best effort, you are at the center of the funnel and the neck is the only way out.

nodes.prompt: 2 · The ladder that precedes the declaration (DAS 2025)
nodes.body: Attempt limits are ceilings, not allowances. If an attempt is not obviously going to work, abandon it early — the counts below are the most you may take, not the number you should.

items.text: Plan A — tracheal intubation. Videolaryngoscope first-line. Maximum 3 + 1 attempts.
items: The +1 is a more experienced operator, not a fourth go by the same person with the same blade.
Change something between attempts — operator, device, position, adjunct — or it is not a new attempt.

items.text: Plan B — second-generation supraglottic airway. Up to 3 attempts.
items: DAS 2025 reframes this as ongoing oxygenation rather than an admission of failure. If it oxygenates, you have time, and time changes everything.
Leaving a supraglottic airway in place also makes the cricothyroid membrane easier to identify.

Plan C — two-person face-mask ventilation, adjuncts in, optimally positioned. Treat failure here as the trigger for Plan D rather than something to persist with; sustained mask ventilation is unlikely once intubation and a supraglottic airway have both failed.
Plan D — declare CICO. Go to the neck.

nodes.prompt: 3 · Declare it, and assign the room
nodes.body: Say it in words the room cannot misread: "This is CICO. I am doing a front-of-neck airway." Then hand out the jobs, because the operator should be doing one thing only.

items: Someone brings the kit — scalpel with a size 10 blade, bougie, 6.0 cuffed tube.
Someone calls for help: ENT, surgery, or the most experienced airway operator in the building. They may not arrive in time, and you start anyway.
Someone keeps oxygen flowing by whatever route still partly works, and someone calls the time out loud.
Someone stops offering the laryngoscope. Once CICO is declared, oscillating back to another look is the failure mode that kills.

nodes.prompt: 4 · Which technique — decided by the patient, not by preference
nodes.body: For an adult, this is not really a choice: scalpel-bougie-tube is the default and the evidence is one-sided. The genuine branch points are age and, to a lesser extent, what is physically in your hand.

items.text: ADULT, and children roughly 8 years and older — SCALPEL-FINGER-BOUGIE. The default.
items: Midline vertical skin incision in every neck under DAS 2025, palpable membrane or not.
In NAP4, cannula cricothyroidotomy failed in roughly 60% of cases while surgical technique was near-uniformly successful. That gap is why there is a default at all.

items.text: UNDER ROUGHLY 8 YEARS — the anatomy changes the answer. See the pediatric card.
items: Neonates and infants: surgical tracheotomy is first-line per the 2024 ESAIC/BJA joint guidelines, which state that surgical cricothyroidotomy and needle cricothyroidotomy are not suitable in this group.
Roughly 1-8 years: surgical tracheotomy preferred where a trained operator is present; percutaneous cricothyroidotomy otherwise.

items.text: CANNULA / NEEDLE — a bridge, not a plan, in adults.
items: Reasonable when it is genuinely the only kit available, when the operator has no surgical training at all, or as a first move in a child while surgical help is coming.
It buys oxygenation at best. It does not protect the airway, cannot take PEEP, and accumulates CO2.

SELDINGER / WIRE-GUIDED KIT — reasonable if your department stocks it and trains on it, and the operator is more fluent in Seldinger technique than in open dissection. Slower than scalpel-bougie in comparative work, and it still needs revision to a definitive airway.

nodes.prompt: 5 · Whatever you did, the next hour is the same
nodes.body: The airway is a bridge. Definitive management, imaging for the complications the procedure causes, documentation of times and attempt counts, and a debrief are all part of the procedure rather than sequelae of it. Each technique card carries its own version of this.

checklist: CICO declared out loud, in words, with the technique named
Jobs assigned: kit, help, oxygen, timekeeper — and someone told to stop offering the laryngoscope
Technique chosen by patient age and anatomy, not by operator preference
Under 8 years: pediatric card opened rather than the adult one
Time of declaration and time of airway noted for the record
buildNote: Entry/decision module for the new CICO & Front-of-Neck Access category. Deliberately does NOT restate any technique — it declares, times, and routes. Each technique lives in its own sibling module so the one you need is one tap away rather than buried in a long page. The attempt ladder is DAS 2025's; the Vortex is included because it is the mental model most ED/ICU teams actually train on and it answers a different question (when have I run out of options?) than the linear algorithm does.
